title: PrefReward: Learning User Preference Matrix for Personalized Text Generation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable ability in generating personalized content by leveraging user histories and contextual cues. However, most existing personalization approaches rely on implicit representations within model parameters, making it difficult to interpret user-specific preferences or effectively handle long-context dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose PrefReward, a novel preference-aware generative framework that explicitly models user styles through a structured preference matrix and integrates it into the decoding process as a reward signal. PrefReward consists of two stages: (1) extracting a user-specific preference matrix that summarizes individual stylistic tendencies, and (2) using the matrix to guide generation via a KL-divergence-based reward function. Experiments on the LongLaMP dataset show that PrefReward outperforms non-personalized and retrieval-based baselines in both generation quality and personalization interpretability.

Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generating fluent, coherent, and context-aware text across a wide range of natural language generation tasks (Salemi et al . , 2024b ; Zhang et al . , 2025c ) . Recently, there has been growing interest in applying LLMs to personalized text generation , where the goal is to adapt the generation process to individual user preferences, historical behaviors, or linguistic styles (Kirk et al . , 2024 ; Mysore et al . , 2023 ; Alhafni et al . , 2024 ) . Such personalization is crucial for applications like dialogue systems, writing assistants, and recommendation-based content generation, where user satisfaction depends heavily on stylistic alignment and contextual relevance (Ji et al . , 2023 ; Kim et al . , 2025 ; He et al . , 2025 ; Zhang et al . , 2025b ) . However, LLM personalization presents several challenges. First , many existing methods require additional training to reliably align model outputs with user preferences — this includes supervised fine-tuning, preference-conditioned adapters, or reinforcement learning procedures. Such training demands labeled preference data, per-user or per-group updates, and substantial compute and engineering effort, which undermines scalability and rapid deployment. Second , current personalization techniques suffer from limited interpretability . Whether preferences are embedded in aligned weights, latent attention over retrieved contexts, or implicitly induced by prompt engineering, the resulting preference signal is typically opaque: it is difficult to inspect which stylistic dimensions the model has learned, to attribute generation behaviors to specific preference factors, or to provide human-understandable explanations and controls. To address these challenges, we propose a new paradigm for personalized generation called PrefReward , which explicitly models and leverages user preferences to guide the decoding process. By introducing an explicit preference representation and a quantitative alignment reward, PrefReward bridges the gap between implicit personalization and controllable stylistic generation. It offers two key advantages: (1) Interpretability : user preferences are represented as visible, human-understandable matrices rather than opaque latent vectors; (2) Train-free personalization : PrefReward operates entirely at the decoding stage without additional fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, making it lightweight and easily applicable to any pretrained LLM backbone. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose PrefReward , a novel reward-guided personalization framework that explicitly models user preferences as interpretable matrices and aligns generation with them through KL-divergence optimization. • We design an efficient preference extraction pipeline combining a BM25-based retriever with token-level LLM inference to capture fine-grained stylistic distributions from user histories. • We conduct extensive experiments on the LongLaMP dataset using Llama2-7B-Chat and the aligned Gemma-2B-IT , demonstrating that PrefReward achieves consistent improvements over retrieval-based baselines in both textual quality and stylistic alignment. 2. Problem Formulation Let 𝒰 \mathcal{U} denote the set of users. Each user u ∈ 𝒰 u\in\mathcal{U} is associated with a profile 𝐏 u \mathbf{P}_{u} containing multiple text samples, representing historical input-output pairs. Given a user u u and an input prompt x x describing a specific task (e.g., composing an email subject), the language model ℳ \mathcal{M} aims to generate an output (1) y ^ = ℳ ​ ( x , 𝐏 u ) , \hat{y}=\mathcal{M}(x,\mathbf{P}_{u}), conditioned on both the prompt x x and the user profile (2) 𝐏 u = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 K . \mathbf{P}_{u}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{K}. Here, each pair ( x i , y i ) (x_{i},y_{i}) encodes a past interaction or text example of the user. The reference output y y represents the desired personalized response, reflecting the unique stylistic patterns of user u u (e.g., customized email drafts or replies). The goal is to ensure that the generated output y ^ \hat{y} not only satisfies the task requirements but also aligns closely with the user-specific writing style inferred from 𝐏 u \mathbf{P}_{u} . Figure 1. Overview of the proposed PrefReward framework, which consists of (1) Preference Matrix Approximation from user profiles and (2) Preference-Guided Decoding using KL-divergence reward. 3. PrefReward In this section, we present our PrefReward framework for personalized text generation as shown in Figure 1 . 3.1. Preference Matrix Extraction Preference Label Selection A central component of our framework is the predefined preference label set 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , which determines the stylistic dimensions captured by the user preference matrix. To construct a label set that is both expressive and interpretable, we take inspiration from the drift framework (Kim et al . , 2025 ) , which advocates defining stylistic attributes as explicit, human-understandable categories instead of relying on latent embedding clusters. Our goal is to build a structured representation 𝐏 u ∈ ℝ K × N \mathbf{P}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times N} , where N N denotes the number of predefined preference labels from a fixed set 𝒫 = { formal , concise , vivid , humor , … } \mathcal{P}=\{\textit{formal},\textit{concise},\textit{vivid},\textit{humor},\ldots\} . Retriever for Profile Selection. Directly using all historical profiles can introduce noise and redundancy, especially for users with long interaction histories. To ensure that only representative and stylistically informative samples are used for preference modeling, we employ a retriever module based on the BM25 ranking algorithm to select the top- K K relevant profiles from ℋ u \mathcal{H}_{u} . Profiles with the highest scores are selected to form ℋ u ∗ = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 K \mathcal{H}^{*}_{u}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{K} , which are then used for preference extraction. Token-Level Preference Extraction. For each text sample, we perform token-wise inference using a pre-trained LLM to compute logits distributions for the next-token prediction. At step i i , we feed ( x , y < i ) (x,y_{<i}) to the model and obtain: p θ ​ ( t i | x , y < i ) = softmax ​ ( LLM ​ ( x , y < i ) ) . p_{\theta}(t_{i}|x,y_{<i})=\text{softmax}(\text{LLM}(x,y_{<i})). We filter the logits to retain only tokens that belong to 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , forming a preference vector 𝐯 i ∈ ℝ N \mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} . Averaging these vectors across all tokens yields a sequence-level preference vector 𝐩 y \mathbf{p}_{y} : 𝐩 y = 1 | y | ​ ∑ i = 1 | y | 𝐯 i . \mathbf{p}_{y}=\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{i=1}^{|y|}\mathbf{v}_{i}. Aggregating the preference vectors across K K samples produces the user preference matrix 𝐏 u = [ 𝐩 y 1 ; … ; 𝐩 y K ] \mathbf{P}_{u}=[\mathbf{p}_{y_{1}};\ldots;\mathbf{p}_{y_{K}}] . Interpretability and Efficiency. This matrix encodes interpretable stylistic preferences—each dimension corresponds to an explicit style or tone. Unlike latent embeddings, 𝐏 u \mathbf{P}_{u} can be directly visualized or compared across users. Computation is efficient since token-level logits are already available during forward passes. 3.2. Preference-Guided Generation KL-Divergence Reward. Given a user u u and their preference matrix 𝐏 u \mathbf{P}_{u} , we generate N c N_{c} candidate outputs { y ( 1 ) , … , y ( N c ) } \{y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(N_{c})}\} for an input x x . Each candidate’s preference vector 𝐩 y ( i ) \mathbf{p}_{y^{(i)}} is derived using the same token-level extraction method. To compute the alignment reward, we first obtain the user’s mean preference distribution: 𝐏 ¯ u = 1 K ​ ∑ j = 1 K 𝐩 y j . \bar{\mathbf{P}}_{u}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbf{p}_{y_{j}}. The reward for each candidate is then computed as: R i = − KL ​ ( 𝐩 y ( i ) ∥ 𝐏 ¯ u ) . R_{i}=-\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\mathbf{p}_{y^{(i)}}\,\big\|\,\bar{\mathbf{P}}_{u}\right). The best candidate is selected as y ∗ = arg ⁡ max i ⁡ R i y^{*}=\arg\max_{i}R_{i} . This reward formulation effectively aligns the generation style with user-specific preferences without retraining the base model. Decoding with Best-of-N Sampling. We employ a Best-of- N c N_{c} strategy: for each prompt, the LLM produces N c N_{c} stochastic generations, and the candidate with the highest reward is chosen. This strategy balances computational cost and personalization quality. 4. Related Work Inspired by the personalization potential of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have explored incorporating user context into generation. Our work is closely related to retrieval- and decoding-based personalization approaches (Zhang et al . , 2025b , a ; Salemi et al . , 2024a ; He et al . , 2025 ; Kim et al . , 2025 ) . Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Salemi et al . , 2024a ) retrieves relevant user profiles via either BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) or Contriever (Lei et al . , 2023 ) matching to provide contextual grounding. However, such retrieval-based personalization often struggles in long-context scenarios where retrieved texts fail to capture consistent user style. Context Steering (CoS) (He et al . , 2025 ) introduces a simple, training-free decoding strategy that amplifies contextual influence by comparing the output probabilities from two forward passes—with and without user context—and linearly scaling their difference. While CoS flexibly controls the degree of personalization, it relies on shallow contextual similarity and lacks explicit preference modeling. Unlike these methods, our proposed PrefReward explicitly constructs user preference matrices and applies KL-divergence-based reward optimization, achieving interpretable and stable personalization across long user histories. 5. Experiments 5.1. Experimental Setup 5.1.1. Datasets. We conduct experiments on the LongLaMP dataset, which provides user-level profiles and historical interaction records with long-context text samples (Kumar et al . , 2024 ) . We focus on the personalized review writing task. For each user, We randomly sample K = 2 K=2 representative profiles per user as the basis for preference extraction. 5.1.2. Baselines. We compare our proposed PrefReward with several representative baselines: • NonPers : Standard LLM generation without any personalization or retrieval augmentation. This baseline evaluates the inherent generative ability of the model. • RAG (BM25) : Retrieval-Augmented Generation using BM25 retriever to fetch relevant user profiles for contextual grounding. It provides a retrieval-based personalization reference (Salemi et al . , 2024a ) . • RAG (CT) : A retrieval-enhanced method that leverages dense embeddings from the Contriever model to retrieve user history semantically (Lei et al . , 2023 ) . • CoS ( λ = 1.0 , 2.0 \lambda=1.0,2.0 ) : Context Steering (CoS) is a training-free decoding method that amplifies user-specific context in generation. It compares outputs with and without context and uses λ \lambda to control the degree of personalization (He et al . , 2025 ) . • PrefReward (Ours) : Our proposed method that first constructs user-specific preference matrices and then applies KL-divergence-based reward optimization to guide decoding. 5.1.3. Evaluation Metrics. Following prior works (Kumar et al . , 2024 ) on personalized generation and retrieval-augmented LLMs, we adopt three widely used evaluation metrics to assess generation quality and personalization effectiveness: ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, and METEOR. 5.1.4. Implementation Details. For zero-shot experiments, we leverage Llama2-7B-Chat as the backbone model. For aligned experiments, we align Gemma-2B-IT using a dataset of (prompt, target output) pairs. During preference extraction, we set the preference label list 𝒫 \mathcal{P} to include 41 stylistic dimensions (e.g., formal , concise , vivid , humor , modest , energy , etc.) following prior work (Kim et al . , 2025 ) . Token-level logits are extracted at each generation step, and the subset corresponding to 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is averaged to form the preference vectors. For reward-guided decoding, we generate N c = 10 N_{c}=10 candidate outputs per prompt using nucleus sampling ( p = 0.95 p=0.95 ) and temperature τ = 0.8 \tau=0.8 . The candidate with the highest KL-based reward is selected as the final output. All models are evaluated on NVIDIA A100 GPU. For the retriever, we employ both the BM25 implementation from rank_bm25 and the Contriever dense retriever from Hugging Face’s facebook/contriever checkpoint. Table 1. Overall Results Table 1 reports the overall performance of all methods on both Llama2-7B-Chat and the aligned Gemma-2B-IT backbone. We evaluate using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, and METEOR, and the following observations can be made: • PrefReward consistently achieves the best performance across both models. On all three metrics, PrefReward surpasses strong personalization baselines, demonstrating that explicit preference matrices combined with KL-divergence reward guidance lead to more faithful and stylistically aligned generation. The gains are stable across backbones, indicating that the proposed method is model-agnostic and generalizes well to different LLM architectures. • RAG and CoS remain limited in long-context personalization. Retrieval-based approaches (BM25 and Contriever) provide moderate improvements—especially on Gemma-2B-IT—but their effectiveness is constrained by retrieval noise and their inability to capture persistent user-level stylistic tendencies. CoS, although training-free and lightweight, relies solely on contextual perturbation and thus struggles to maintain stable personalization when user histories grow longer or more complicated. Overall, these findings confirm that explicitly modeling user preferences and leveraging them as decoding rewards provide a more effective and interpretable solution for long-context personalized generation. 5.3. Effect of Preference Label Size To investigate how the number of preference labels influences model performance, we vary the size of the preference list used to construct the preference matrix, Figure 2 reports the corresponding results on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, and METEOR. These results demonstrate that enlarging the preference label set enhances personalization quality, but excessive preference dimensions bring diminishing returns. In practice, selecting around 20 representative preference labels strikes an effective balance between expressiveness and efficiency. Figure 2. Effect of different preference label size on model performance 5.4. Case Study Figure 3 presents qualitative examples comparing the outputs of baseline models and our PrefReward framework. The PrefReward output closely aligns with the ground-truth review, accurately capturing key user sentiments. By leveraging explicit preference matrices and KL-based reward guidance, PrefReward produces text that is not only more faithful to the user’s style but also avoids unnecessary hallucinations, demonstrating stronger controllability and interpretability in personalized generation. Figure 3. Case study of personalized generation in LongLaMP 6. Conclusion We introduced PrefReward , a preference-aware framework for personalized text generation. By explicitly modeling user preferences as interpretable matrices and integrating them via KL-divergence rewards, PrefReward bridges the gap between personalization quality and transparency. Experiments confirm its superiority over retrieval-based and non-personalized baselines. Future work will explore fine-tuning LLMs with preference-aware reinforcement learning for end-to-end optimization. References (1) Alhafni et al .
